items.stem:
Tanvi compares bird lists: Colombia ~1,400 species, India >1,200, New York 105 and Greenland 56.
(i) What pattern does this show? (1 mark)
(ii) Give one reason for it. (1 mark)
(iii) For areas within a region, Z ≈ 0.1–0.2. What does Z represent, and when is it much steeper? (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Latitudinal gradient: diversity decreases from the equator to the poles. (ii) Tropics were undisturbed for long periods, less seasonal, or receive more solar energy (any one). (iii) Z is the slope of the line (regression coefficient) of log S against log A; it is steeper (0.6–1.2) for very large areas such as whole continents.

items.stem: Explain the rivet popper hypothesis.
items.answer: Paul Ehrlich compared an ecosystem to an airplane and species to rivets. Removing a few rivets (species) may not affect flight safety initially, but as more are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak; loss of rivets on key parts (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is more serious than on less important parts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark analogy; 1 mark key species.

items.answer: (i) Alien species invasion. (ii) It threatens the indigenous catfishes of Indian rivers. (iii) India: Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana or water hyacinth (Eichhornia); Africa: Nile perch in Lake Victoria, which caused extinction of more than 200 cichlid species.

items.stem: Explain co-extinction with two examples.
items.answer: When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct. Examples: when a host fish species becomes extinct its unique assemblage of parasites meets the same fate; co-evolved plant–pollinator mutualism, where extinction of one invariably leads to extinction of the other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark definition; 1 mark examples.

items.stem: What is the "evil quartet"? Describe each cause of biodiversity loss with an example.
items.answer: (i) Habitat loss and fragmentation – tropical rain forests reduced from 14% to 6% of land; Amazon cleared for soybean and cattle pastures. (ii) Over-exploitation – Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon became extinct; marine fish overharvested. (iii) Alien species invasions – Nile perch in Lake Victoria caused extinction of over 200 cichlid species; Parthenium, Lantana, water hyacinth; African catfish Clarias gariepinus. (iv) Co-extinctions – parasites of a host fish, plant–pollinator mutualism.

items.answer: (i) In situ. (ii) Tribal communities protect them because of religious beliefs, so trees and wildlife are not cut or hunted. items.stem: Why should we conserve biodiversity? Describe in situ and ex situ methods of conservation with examples.
items.answer: Reasons: narrowly utilitarian (food, fibre, medicines, bioprospecting), broadly utilitarian (ecosystem services – the Amazon produces about 20% of total oxygen; pollination; aesthetics) and ethical (intrinsic value of every species). In situ: protecting the whole ecosystem – biodiversity hotspots, biosphere reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and sacred groves (Khasi and Jaintia Hills, Aravalli Hills, Western Ghats). Ex situ: zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation of gametes, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture and seed banks.
items.markingKey: 2 marks reasons; 1.5 marks in situ; 1.5 marks ex situ.
